data.title: Environmental groups embrace AI, even as they warn of data center impacts
data.description: WASHINGTON, Nov 7 : Environmental groups worldwide are using artificial intelligence to analyze climate data, track forest fires and count endangered wildlife – embracing a technology they also warn is driving a surge in electricity demand, water use and greenhouse-gas emissions. The contradiction is forcing these organizations to justify their AI use in carrying out missions to combat climate change or protect natural resources. "We recognize that AI can come with environmental costs, and we need to be thoughtful about how we use it," said Ali Swanson, AI lead at the US nonprofit Conservation International. "But at a time when the climate and biodiversity crises are becoming more urgent, AI can help us move faster and make better use of the information we're collecting." The group recently started using AI to assess hotspots detected by satellites and send real-time alerts to community forest patrols about potential wildfires in remote and environmentally sensitive parts of Cambodia. Reuters interviewed 15 major environmental, conservation and development organizations about their AI use. All said they used the technology in some form and expressed concern about the environmental impact of the data centers powering it. The centers, filled with servers, can require vast amounts of electricity, along with water for cooling. It's a global dilemma for individuals, governments and industries balancing AI's benefits with its enormous risks. The tradeoffs likely will grab attention at the UN's COP31 climate conference this month, when host Turkey will call on governments, businesses and other institutions to sign a pledge outlining principles to ensure AI is developed and deployed sustainably. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres wants major AI companies to publicly disclose their systems' environmental impacts. Researchers at the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health estimate the global data-center footprint could more than double by 2030, reaching a size about twice that of Jakarta, the Indonesian megalopolis. The International Energy Agency, meanwhile, estimates global data centers will consume about 945 terawatt-hours of electricity annually by 2030, producing the equivalent of more than 300 million metric tons of carbon dioxide. That's double current consumption and about equal to Japan's annual electricity use. The agency also projects that global data center water consumption will increase from about 560 billion liters (147.9 billion gallons) in 2023 to about 1.2 trillion liters (317 billion gallons) annually by 2030. Technology giants including Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet's Google have reported rising emissions linked in part to data center expansion, raising questions about their ability to meet their own long-term climate goals. Amazon told Reuters its artificial-intelligence products were among the most sustainable due to the company's purchases of low-carbon energy and its efforts to use power and water efficiently. Microsoft and Google didn't respond to requests for comment. BREAKTHROUGHS ONCE THOUGHT IMPOSSIBLE Many of the organizations that spoke to Reuters believe AI's benefits currently outweigh its costs because the technology is enabling work that was previously difficult, expensive or impossible. Kenya's Save the Elephants, a partner of the Wildlife Conservation Network, said it is using machine learning to improve population surveys and study elephant communication. Frank Pope, the group's chief executive, said an aerial survey of Kenya's largest protected area last year generated roughly 200,000 images that took nine people nine months to review manually. AI models trained on Nvidia's GeForce graphics platforms can now complete similar analyses in hours. "The results have been eye-opening," Pope said. "We found that human surveys were missing about a third of the elephants, roughly half of zebras and giraffes, and three-quarters of oryx populations." More accurate wildlife data can help secure financing for conservation, he said. "Ultimately, these tools make nature measurable and therefore investable," he said. "That's a critical transformation, if we're going to conserve biodiversity at scale." At the institute founded by the late conservation icon Jane Goodall, researchers are using AI to digitize decades of field notes about chimpanzee behavior in Tanzania's Gombe National Park. The project was once expected to take 13-15 years because the records were written by hand using the local Kiha language and scientific shorthand. Thanks to a tool developed with Amazon Web Services, the notes can now be scanned, translated and structured in minutes, slashing the time needed to about two years, said Lilian Pintea, the Jane Goodall Institute's vice president of conservation science. During her lifetime, Pintea said, Goodall supported the use of AI to advance conservation science, provided people remained firmly in control of how it was used. "AI technology should be seen as tools which are human-centered," Pintea said. LIMITING THE ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT Some organizations are experimenting with ways to limit the environmental impact of their AI use. The World Resources Institute (WRI), a research group that uses AI to accelerate its climate and environmental analyses, said it limits resource-intensive applications such as generating videos and images, while caching AI query results so identical searches don't need to be reprocessed. The US-based Nature Conservancy has adopted a similar approach. It uses AI to analyze video captured on commercial fishing vessels for information on how many fish of different species they catch. But instead of uploading huge numbers of videos to centralized data centers, it has installed AI-powered digital cameras to process information aboard the vessels, reducing energy use and data-transfer requirements, said Vienna Saccomanno, a senior scientist at the organization. "It takes a lot of engineering to make computation on the edge possible," she said. "This was worth it to reduce both our carbon footprint and deliver these sustainability insights." Greenpeace International said it, too, uses some AI tools, mainly because software platforms it relies upon include AI features. It's imposing internal guidelines emphasizing transparency, human oversight and "intentional" AI use, the group said. But it would prefer to sidestep the technology due to its environmental impacts and is pushing back hard on the data center buildout. "While other organizations are asking how to use AI responsibly, Greenpeace is asking whether it's necessary to build all these massive data centers in the first place," said Katrin Xueying Wu, a climate and energy campaigner with the organization. Other groups now see AI as vital to effective environmental activism. "It's our job to save the planet. If we can do that more effectively and efficiently with the limited resources we've got by using AI, then we have to seriously engage in that possibility," said Stuart Butchart, chief scientist at UK-based BirdLife International. "If we don't do it, then we're sort of being derelict in our duty." (Additonal reporting by Simon Jessop in London and Kate Abnett in Brussels; Editing by Richard Valdmanis and Alexandra Zavis)

data.title: Google executive Donald Harrison resigns from SpaceX board
data.description: Nov 6 : SpaceX disclosed on Friday that Google executive Donald Harrison has resigned from the rockets-to-AI company's board after more than a decade. Here are some details: • Harrison notified SpaceX of his resignation on November 4, and it took effect immediately • The Elon Musk-led company said Harrison's decision to resign was not due to any disagreement with the company on matters relating to its operations, policies or practices • Harrison, a longtime executive at Google, is currently president of Global Partnerships and Corporate Development. Google parent Alphabet is the ‌largest single institutional holder of SpaceX, according to LSEG data • Musk said that Harrison stepped down because there were too many conflicts of interest with Alphabet. "Don has been a great board member. Very much appreciate his contributions," Musk added in a post on X on Friday. • Google on Friday reported a small increase in its position in SpaceX to about 555 million shares from 551.2 million earlier

data.title: After years of robust growth, a tough 2027 ahead for Singapore banks: Analysts
data.description: SINGAPORE: Despite the prospect of higher interest rates, Singapore banks may face a tougher environment in 2027, analysts told CNA. “The boom years did a lot of the work for Singapore’s banks,” said Mr Eric Xiao, head of sales in Asia for CMC Markets. “In 2027, they’ll have to do it themselves.” He said it appears to be more difficult to cash in on the wealth boom than expected, noting that DBS took in a record S$15 billion (US$11.7 billion) of net new money for the third quarter of the year and still saw wealth fees fall 6 per cent because clients traded less. Banks will eventually benefit from higher interest rates, he said, but margin income could get squeezed initially because rates on deposits tend to rise more quickly than rates on loans. Overall, he does not expect the banks to see a “down year” despite the difficult conditions ahead. Mr Ritesh Ganeriwal, group head of investment and advisory at Syfe, said the banks’ core business held up in Q3, but “the problem is that interest rates are no longer doing the heavy lifting”. Even with interest rates in the US rising, Singapore rates have stayed low, and banks are competing harder for deposits, so margins are getting squeezed. “That points to slower growth in 2027, driven by loans and wealth fees, rather than a downturn,” he said. Their comments came after the three local banks reported earnings for Q3 2026, with the financial results for DBS and UOB falling short of expectations. OCBC’s net profit, reported on Friday (Nov 6), grew 3 per cent to S$2.04 billion, beating analysts’ estimates of its performance. DBS saw its net profit for July to August fall 5 per cent from a year ago to S$2.81 billion, while UOB’s net profit increased 182 per cent to S$1.25 billion, but missed expectations. The spike in UOB’s net profit came off a low base, as the bank set aside S$1.36 billion in allowances for credit and other losses in the third quarter of last year.The banks’ share prices have also been under pressure in recent weeks, along with the broader Singapore market, after climbing rapidly in the earlier part of the year. “The recent sell-off appears to reflect a combination of earnings disappointment and weaker macroeconomic sentiment,” said an analyst from digital brokerage MooMoo. Further earnings weakness, deteriorating credit conditions or prolonged macroeconomic pressures could weigh on performance and share price, they added. However, credit quality, loan growth and wealth management remain key factors in the medium-term investment outlook, said the analyst. DIVERGING PATHS? Looking ahead to 2027, analysts also noted that the banks are not in equal positions. “DBS has the steadiest outlook,” said Mr Cheng Chye Hsern, head of investment at Providend. The bank’s management said net interest income has bottomed out, with mid-single-digit growth of total income expected next year. It has the highest profitability, but its share price is nearly three times its book value, compared with its historical average of 1.6 times. Mr Xiao of CMC Markets said DBS and UOB have different reasons for missing analysts’ expectations. For DBS, the shortfall came from markets trading income plunging 65 per cent, signalling a rough quarter on the desks rather than any deeper issues, he said. However, UOB's problem is harder to fix, he said: “Margins are thinner, and costs keep rising into 2027." OCBC said it expects loan growth to be in the low double digits for this year, and that it is well placed for higher rates. But its insurance arm, Great Eastern, will keep group earnings lumpier whenever bond markets move sharply, said Mr Cheng of Providend.Ms Joanna Cheah, ASEAN research analyst at Jefferies, said earnings drivers are becoming more differentiated between the local lenders. UOB faces greater earnings pressure from persistent net interest margin compression, while DBS and OCBC’s net interest margins started to recover at the end of the third quarter, she said. ARE BANKS AFFECTING THE BROADER MARKET? Analysts said that while the three local lenders form a very large part of the Straits Times Index and will affect its direction significantly, the recent decline in the index is not purely a bank story. Ms Cheah attributes the current weakness partly to a global risk-off sentiment, and partly to some domestic profit-taking after a strong rally. The US midterm elections outcome earlier this week accelerated the sell-off amid concerns that greater regulatory scrutiny could slow investment into artificial intelligence and data centre industries. “That has spilled into Asian markets, including Singapore,” she said, noting that the decline locally has broadened beyond financials. “We would distinguish this market volatility from Singapore fundamentals, which remain relatively defensive, supported by resilient earnings, a strong currency and healthy corporate balance sheets,” she said.

data.title: OpenAI gets $11 billion funding at $1.25 trillion valuation, source says
data.description: Nov 6 : OpenAI has closed on new funding of $11 billion, the initial part of a round that values the company at $1.25 trillion, a source familiar with the matter said on Friday. The $11 billion raised so far represents only a portion of OpenAI's original target of up to $30 billion, while the company's valuation has come down from the $1.5 trillion level it had initially sought, two investors said. SoftBank and MGX participated in the funding, the investors said. Bloomberg News reported on the funding earlier on Friday. Sentiment toward AI companies has cooled in the last month, with some investors valuing rival Anthropic's planned IPO at about $1.5 trillion, below earlier expectations of roughly $2 trillion.

data.title: Tech stocks stage partial rebound while dollar gains after US jobs data
data.description: NEW YORK: Tech shares rose Friday (Nov 6), recovering a fraction of losses from the prior session's rout as the dollar rallied after better-than-expected US jobs data.   Investors welcomed a partial recovery for the tech-heavy Nasdaq after its plunge on Thursday, which sent Asian and European markets tumbling.   But the Nasdaq technically entered a correction after dropping more than 10 per cent over the past month, reflecting worries that sweeping victories by Democrats in this week's US elections would slow or derail the artificial intelligence data centre buildout.   After slumping 5.5 per cent on Thursday, the tech-focused Nasdaq clawed back 1.1 per cent on Friday.   "Markets could receive an additional boost if the Democrats soften their tone on AI," said a note from Jose Torres of Interactive Brokers.    In a CNN interview, Texas Governor-elect Gina Hiojasa, among the newly elected leaders that spotlighted the issue during the campaign, said communities need more say on if and where data centres get built.   "We have always been a pro-business state in Texas, but what changes now with me as governor is it has to be a partnership that benefits Texans," she said. "It is not that I hate data centres; I hate the way they are taking advantage of Texas, and that stops when I'm governor."   Investors were encouraged by a report showing that the US economy added 165,000 jobs last month, far more than analysts had expected. While the US jobs data - including a dip in the unemployment rate to 4.1 per cent - reassured investors on the strength of the economy, it also cleared the way for the US Federal Reserve to raise interest rates.Investors widely expect the Fed to raise interest rates by a quarter percentage point at its next meeting in December to bring down stubborn inflation. Those expectations were also reflected in the foreign exchange market, with the dollar rising against the euro and other major currencies. "The prospect of a relatively more aggressive Federal Reserve has moved back into focus, making it increasingly difficult for the euro to recover ground consistently," said a note from Julian Pineda, a market analyst at Forex.com.  Rising interest rates would further complicate the calculus for tech firms that have propelled markets worldwide over a four-year bull run. "Big worries are colliding - the build-out of data centres looks set to slow, which risks shredding the spending spree underpinning the boom, right at the time that investors have become super nervous about returns on this massive investment," said Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club. The Tokyo and Seoul stock markets closed out their weeks with losses of 6 per cent following the Nasdaq's 5.5 per cent collapse on Thursday, its worst showing since April last year when Trump unveiled his wide-ranging global tariffs. On Seoul's Kospi stocks index, chip giant SK hynix slumped 10 per cent and its rival Samsung lost 6.4 per cent. The London, Paris and Frankfurt stock markets finished down, despite featuring few technology firms.

data.title: Wall Street stocks rally after heavy AI-related selloff
data.description: NEW YORK/LONDON, Nov 6 : Wall Street equities mostly rallied on Friday, reversing course after trillions of dollars of world stock market value were wiped out over fears that Democratic election victories this week would bring tighter US regulations for the AI industry. The benchmark S&P 500 and the Nasdaq finished higher, with technology, communication services and industrials stocks driving gains. The Dow ended lower. All three indexes notched weekly losses following a brutal selloff in the prior session. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.46 per cent, the S&P 500 rose 0.31 per cent, and the Nasdaq Composite gained 1.1 per cent. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index was up 4.2 per cent after slumping in its biggest one-day drop since April 2025. Nvidia rose nearly 3 per cent, after its worst day since January 2025, when the emergence of low-cost Chinese AI model DeepSeek hammered markets. Other heavyweight chipmakers, including AMD, Intel, and Micron Technology, closed up between 5 per cent and 11 per cent, while Elon Musk's Tesla and SpaceX were also up 4 per cent and nearly 9 per cent respectively after losses earlier this week. "Most of the disruption of the AI buildout will not probably occur but it's just the uncertainty of the change in government from Republican-led to Democratic-led, not only at the federal level but the state, local levels," said Gerry Sparrow, president and portfolio manager at Sparrow Capital Management. "That's causing some disruption in the expectations of investors ... The volatility around elections or any political event, whether it be war or terrorist attack, is always going to disrupt the market." Texas' Democratic Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa said on Thursday that the state — which already has a large share of US data centres — will introduce new laws to protect local communities from their further mass buildup. The jitters are hitting an AI trade already under pressure from fears that the massive cost of the data centres and other infrastructure will limit future returns, spurring margin calls and spooking retail investors and hedge funds alike. RIPPLE EFFECT The bounces were in stark contrast with market action in the rest of the world. Europe's STOXX 600 lost 1 per cent. In Asia, Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's KOSPI both slumped about 6 per cent. For the Nikkei — just like Wall Street the previous day — it was the biggest one-day drop since US President Donald Trump's "Liberation Day" trade tariff panic of April 2025. The MSCI All-World index fell 0.68 per cent while MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan lost nearly 3 per cent. PAYROLLS BEAT FORECASTS US nonfarm payrolls, usually one of the most-watched pieces of data, but largely overshadowed by the tech drama, showed a stronger-than-expected 165,000 pickup in jobs. An anticipated slowdown in annual wage growth to below 3 per cent for the first time in nearly 5-1/2 years did not materialise either, as it came in at 3.1 per cent. The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note ticked up to 4.86 per cent, having dropped to its lowest level since September 9 overnight. In currencies, the dollar rose against major currencies including the euro, yen and Swiss franc. It was up 0.52 per cent against the yen and rose 0.47 per cent against the Swiss franc. The euro was down 0.68 per cent against the dollar at $1.1142. Brent crude prices settled at $98.32, rising just 0.03 per cent, on hopes the midterms' results might prompt Trump to de-escalate the Iran war. Spot gold was flat at $4,066.28 per ounce.

data.title: Commentary: Is the AI stock bubble finally bursting?
data.description: LONDON: This is getting faintly ridiculous now. Yet again, tech stocks are being hit hard - the third shakeout in just the past few weeks. But this is more worrisome than previous outbreaks of nerves. Once more, but this time with feeling, investors are asking: “Is this the big one? Is the AI bubble finally bursting?” I don’t claim to know the answer. Ask me again in a week or so, and we will know if this wobble deepens and broadens or if it is yet another head fake. But the fact that we’re all asking the same question yet again is very telling in itself. It is clear that AI technology works. No argument there. But the internet worked out pretty well, and it still crashed the markets a quarter of a century ago. (Sorry if that makes you feel old.) Any reasonable person can see the hallmarks of an unsustainable party in AI assets, perhaps most conspicuously in AI-related stocks, which truly dominate US and global markets. Pick from a list of possible sources of stress, including high levels of increasingly creatively structured debt, questionable levels of true revenue potential, and head-scratching examples of circular financing.AI WAS ON THE US BALLOT PAPER As the Bank for International Settlements recently pointed out, nearly 29 per cent of AI firms’ investment deals are in other AI firms, and more than half of incoming investment in AI firms comes from other AI firms. In a crisis, circular financing can easily turn into a circular firing squad.  All of this has been true and widely accepted to be the potential nexus of a correction for months. We have just never really known what would be the trigger. US politics may finally be that thing. The initial reaction to this week’s historic US midterm elections, which delivered thumping victories for the Democratic Party across Congress and in state-level positions, was very positive.  Stocks sailed higher all around the world, partly in relief that the result was unambiguous and uncontested, partly in hope that we could make markets normal again with stronger checks and balances to a capricious president, and partly on the sense that the elections could bring forward the end to the apparently senseless war in Iran. The price of oil tumbled under US$100 a barrel, having stood as high as US$118 at the end of last month, after voters across the US sent a strong message that they were fed up with war-driven high energy prices jacking up the cost of living (and of driving). The market’s judgment is that one way or another, the war has to end, and fast. But the good vibes in markets lasted all of a day. That is because the other thing voters made clear was that they do not like AI, and specifically that they do not want enormous energy- and water-guzzling data centres built in their neighbourhoods.  AI itself was on the ballot across multiple states, with measures seeking views from voters on whether to delay or restrict data centre developments. Voters stuck up two fingers at Big Tech almost every time. A much tougher regulatory and permitting framework lies ahead for a sector holding up an alarming amount of sky in the US economy and in global markets.Frank Flight, a strategist at Citadel Securities, said in a note on Thursday that in theory, at least some of these projects will simply shift from unfriendly to friendly states. They still end up happening. Maybe. But this is still a problem for projects financed with huge amounts of borrowed money.  “Securing alternative sites, power and approvals takes time, so this adjustment could still materially delay deployment and raise costs,” he said. “We would therefore expect some moderation in the near-term growth and inflation impulse from construction and associated resource demand, alongside a smaller impact on cumulative investment and financing requirements.” Diversified technology companies, particularly those with data centre capacity already tied up, are faring relatively well in the latest burst of stress, which on Thursday (Nov 5) dragged the techy Nasdaq Composite 5 per cent, its biggest fall in 19 months. But pure-play AI build-out bets have taken a real beating. CoreWeave stocks fell 10 per cent on Thursday alone, taking their decline since the peak in May to 70 per cent. Chips maker Sandisk fell 22 per cent on Thursday. Micron dropped 17 per cent. “At these valuations, the AI trade is like a shark that has to keep swimming to stay alive,” said Trevor Greetham, head of multi-asset at Royal London Asset Management.WHAT A TRUE AI CRASH COULD LOOK LIKE Before the midterms, in October, Dario Perkins at research house TS Lombard sketched out what a true crash in the AI trade might look like. Naturally, a lot of this is guesswork, but he reckons a worst-case scenario could wipe at least 30 per cent off US stocks and spark up to US$200 billion in credit losses, with “a wave” of tech-related debt defaults. For stocks, “these are conservative estimates, which take the tech share of the US market back to pre-ChatGPT days”, he said. Government bonds and non-US stocks stand out as potential refuges, he added. It is a sobering analysis, but plausible too - tellingly, US Treasury bonds have already turned higher. A swift end to the war in Iran still stands as the best chance for markets to regain a solid footing.  But one day, the alarm from the AI trade will not be a drill.

data.title: Google acquires Wyoming data center site from AI infrastructure firm Crusoe
data.description: Nov 6 : Google has acquired Crusoe's data center site in southeast Wyoming, the AI infrastructure developer said on Friday, a day after the Alphabet unit announced a $17-billion investment in the project. Here are some details: • Google announced the investment on Thursday to build its first data center in Wyoming, expanding its AI infrastructure despite growing political opposition to such projects in parts of the US • Crusoe said it has completed its involvement in the project's pre-development phase, which included site selection, government approvals and power strategy • The deal's financial terms were not disclosed • The campus was initially developed by Crusoe and Tallgrass Energy • Google on Thursday said it would build the facility in partnership with Tallgrass Energy, as well as Black Hills Energy, American Electric Power and Related Digital • Crusoe Chief Executive Chase Lochmiller said the company has more than 6 gigawatts of contracted capacity and over 40 gigawatts in its development pipeline • Crusoe added that it is developing another Google data center campus in Armstrong, which it announced earlier this year

data.title: USDA to launch AI tool to check crop production data after errors
data.description: CHICAGO, Nov 6 : The US Department of Agriculture will use an artificial intelligence tool it built to check data in next week's monthly crop production report, agency officials said, after a series of data missteps eroded farmers' and traders' trust in its forecasts. After the USDA discovered errors in its corn data from September, officials determined the AI tool would have flagged the problem and decided to use it on the crop production report due on November 10, USDA Under Secretary Scott Hutchins said in an interview. The tool's debut tests whether the agency can restore confidence in data that often moves markets.  "I'm very bullish on the fact that we'll be able to utilize these tools in the future to help us avoid these kinds of really, truly unfortunate errors," Hutchins said on Thursday. Last month, the USDA corrected its September corn production and yield data. The correction raised the yield estimate by about 3 per cent in Nebraska, the third-biggest corn-producing state, and lowered it by about 2 per cent in Kansas.  The agency, long viewed as the gold standard of global agricultural market information, previously faced criticism after it made sharp upward revisions to estimates for last year's corn acreage. Over the summer, it  reported inaccurate beef export sales data. The USDA previously said it was launching a pilot project that would rely more heavily on technology to improve crop acreage and yield estimates as fewer farmers respond to its surveys.  COMPUTER FILE ERROR  Lance Honig, chair of the agricultural statistics board for USDA's National Agricultural Statistics Service, told Reuters that a computer file incorrectly combined data on irrigated and non-irrigated corn acres gathered by field surveyors, causing the errors in September's data. Kansas and Nebraska were affected because they have higher percentages of irrigated fields, which often have higher yields, he said.  "This error that occurred in September is literally a very isolated occurrence that, quite frankly, with the proper validation, we should have caught," Honig said. "There was no issue with the data that was gathered at the field level." The errors angered farmers who are struggling to make money as they pay soaring prices for diesel, fertilizer and other inputs. Last month, the National Corn Growers Association, which represents 35,000 farmers, said the September errors were unacceptable and had further hurt farmers' confidence in the USDA's ability to produce accurate reports. "You just don't know what the USDA is going to do anymore," said Jim Gerlach, president of brokerage A/C Trading in Indiana, on Friday. "Their reports have become so erratic." Questions around the credibility of federal data increased after President Donald Trump's administration sharply downsized the government last year. Thousands of employees at the USDA have left, and experts have worried the cuts hobbled the agency's ability to produce accurate and timely data. Hutchins said the September errors were not related to staffing losses. The new AI tool will add to, not replace, the agency's data validation, he said.  "The tool is basically going to be used as a check to make sure that there are no anomalies that we were not able to see or identify in the normal process," Hutchins said.       This week, market analysts questioned the accuracy of another monthly USDA report on soy processing which showed a sharp divide between how many soybeans were crushed and how much soymeal was produced in Iowa.  The USDA said it was reviewing the report as part of a normal process and would make any necessary revisions next month.

data.title: OpenAI to press ahead with data-center expansion despite midterm sweep, CFO tells CNBC
data.description: Nov 6 : OpenAI will press ahead with its US data-center expansion plans despite a Democratic midterm sweep this week that has fueled fears of tighter scrutiny of the facilities, its Chief Financial Officer Sarah Friar told CNBC in an interview on Friday. "When I think about the midterms, I need to keep thinking about how do we keep investing to meet customer demand," Friar said. "We are going to keep building out those relationships with communities so we can get the compute we need," she added.  One of the corporate faces of the AI boom, OpenAI has moved quickly to counter fears that a shift in congressional power could slow the industry's growth. It launched a charm offensive on Thursday to win over communities as opposition to data centers becomes a rallying point for anxieties about the technology. As part of the efforts, OpenAI said, it will no longer use non-disclosure agreements with public officials when negotiating or discussing future sites. It will also give residents access to construction plans ⁠and their potential effects. Growing data-center opposition was a crucial issue in the midterm elections. Democratic candidates, including Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, made tighter scrutiny of the facilities a central campaign pledge. The Lone Star State is one of the fastest-growing data-center regions in the world. Fears the Democratic sweep may slow construction of the facilities critical to the AI boom wiped about $2.5 trillion off the US stock market on Thursday, as investors weighed the fallout for the chip, cloud and networking industries that have been among the biggest beneficiaries of the spending frenzy. Still, there are signs that tech giants remain committed to data-center expansion plans despite the growing backlash. Alphabet-owned Google said on Thursday it would invest $17 billion to build its first data center in Wyoming. Meanwhile, Bloomberg News reported that ByteDance is considering expanding a data center project in northeastern Brazil, a move that would strengthen its standing as Latin America's leading builder of computing facilities. OPENAI'S FUNDRAISING PLANS Friar also told CNBC that OpenAI was raising fresh capital, pushing back against suggestions the ChatGPT maker had scaled back its fundraising ambitions amid the sharp AI stocks selloff. The company is seeking fresh capital after its business grew 70 per cent quarter over quarter in the third quarter, with enterprise demand doubling over the same period, she said. "It (the growth) is saying people are actually using AI and getting value from it," Friar said. The fundraising comes as the market turmoil is raising questions about OpenAI rival Anthropic's widely awaited listing. Reuters reported on Thursday that prospective investors in Anthropic's IPO are questioning whether the AI startup can begin its roadshow next week and stay on track for a November listing. Investors are pushing ‌for a more attractive valuation to commit to the offering, with some viewing the recently discussed $1.5 trillion valuation as being at the high end of expectations, four people familiar with investor discussions told Reuters.

data.title: Nubank, Mercado Pago halt crypto transfers after external provider disruption
data.description: SAO PAULO, Nov 6 : Brazilian digital lender Nubank and Mercado Pago, the fintech arm from MercadoLibre, have halted some cryptocurrency transfers due to disruptions from an external data provider, the companies said in separate statements on Friday. • Nubank said it has halted cryptocurrency withdrawals and deposits • Mercado Pago said it blocked some transfers to external wallets, and added that deposits could also face delays • Both companies said client funds remain secure, and that other crypto products continue to operate as usual • Neither company identified the external provider involved, and it was unclear whether both were affected by the same provider • Nubank cited "instability from an external data provider," while Mercado Pago mentioned "an incident affecting a risk monitoring and anti-money laundering service provider" • Last week, hackers targeted exchange Binance to drain $6.3 billion worth of crypto, the largest such heist on record

data.title: Microsoft is winding down Oracle deal to rent AI cloud capacity, Bloomberg News reports
data.description: Nov 6 : Microsoft is winding down an arrangement to rent AI computing from Oracle as part of a larger reassessment of billions of dollars in cloud partnerships, Bloomberg News reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter. Oracle shares were down nearly 3 per cent in afternoon trading, while Microsoft was little changed.  Microsoft has been turning off rented computing capacity from Oracle in recent months after declining to renew the contract, according to the report. Over time, the computing capacity Microsoft was renting became less valuable as it no longer met the company's evolving needs, the report added. Microsoft and Oracle did not immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comment.
